narrative:
The model predicts you have a 22% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your number of past class failures, your weekly study time, and whether you attended nursery school. Past failures had the biggest impact and pushed the prediction toward passing because you have had none at all, matching the average of students who succeeded. However, your very low weekly study time worked against you and was the second strongest influence, pulling the outcome toward failure. Most students who passed dedicated 2–5 hours per week, while you spend less than 2. Not having attended nursery school also nudged the prediction slightly toward failing, though this was the smallest of the three effects; only about one in five successful students had the same background.

Taken together, the model sees your clean record on failures as helpful, but your limited study habits and early education gap as enough of a risk to justify extra support. To improve, you should focus first on building a consistent study routine of at least two hours most days. Consider talking with your teachers about targeted help in any subjects that have felt shaky. Small, steady changes in how you prepare can shift your trajectory before the final exams. (218 words)
